articles.title: SFR Binding MOU Signed: France's €20.35B Consolidation Is Now a Matter of Execution
articles.subtitle: Orange CEO's 'behavioral remedies' signal ahead of filing points to Phase 2 antitrust scrutiny, not a fast-track clearance.
articles.body_md:
France's mobile market restructuring cleared its most critical commercial milestone on June 6, 2026, when **Bouygues Telecom**, **Orange**, and **Free-iliad** signed a binding Memorandum of Understanding with **Altice France** for the €20.35B acquisition of **SFR** — one day after the June 5 exclusivity deadline expired.

## From Exclusivity to Economic Commitment

The MOU is structurally different from the exclusivity agreement it replaces. It establishes economic terms, asset divisions, and break-up fees — reported in the range of **€100M–€2B** — materially raising the cost of exit above any prior milestone in this process. The asset split is confirmed: Bouygues Telecom takes 42% of the purchase price (~€8.5B) and 52% of SFR revenue, including B2B and rural mobile. Free-iliad absorbs 31% (~€6.3B) and 27% of revenue. Orange takes 27% (~€5.5B) and 21% of revenue.

For infrastructure investors, the binding MOU sharply reduces deal collapse probability. Two prior deadline extensions — May 15 and June 5 — created uncertainty that is now resolved by a signed instrument with financial penalties for withdrawal.

## Regulatory Timeline: Why Heydemann's Comment Matters

The **Autorité de la concurrence** clock starts only when definitive legal documents are formally filed — requiring final binding agreements expected H2 2026, with regulatory closing targeted H2 2027. Orange CEO **Christel Heydemann** publicly referenced "behavioral remedies" before formal notification. That framing is significant: it signals the consortium expects Phase 2 engagement or a remedies negotiation rather than the permissive Phase 1 fast-track that EU Draft Revised Merger Guidelines theoretically enable for capital-intensive infrastructure deals.

The French market's regulatory dynamics differ from Romania and the UK, both cleared without Phase 2. The Autorité de la concurrence has historically imposed structural remedies in mobile consolidation: spectrum reallocation, MVNO wholesale access terms, and tower-sharing obligations. Bouygues's 52% revenue share — the largest of three acquirers — will draw particular scrutiny on B2B market structure.

## Implications Through H2 2027

**Altice France**'s €40B+ debt load — the original forcing function behind three deadline extensions — remains under creditor scrutiny through the H2 2027 closing. Network integration capex, spectrum strategy, and rural mobile investment planning are effectively in suspension for 12–18 months pending clearance.

Watch: formal notification date to the Autorité de la concurrence (requires definitive documents, H2 2026); Altice France bond pricing as a creditor confidence signal; and the structural remedies package, particularly spectrum reallocation terms and MVNO wholesale access conditions.
articles.summary: Bouygues, Orange, and Free-iliad signed a binding MOU with Altice France on June 6 for the €20.35B acquisition of SFR, establishing break-up fees in the €100M–€2B range. Orange CEO's pre-notification reference to 'behavioral remedies' signals Phase 2 antitrust engagement with the Autorité de la concurrence, with regulatory closing targeted H2 2027.

articles.title: SoftBank Commits €75B to France AI Data Centres: Europe's Largest Infrastructure Pledge
articles.subtitle: The €45B Phase 1 requires 3.1 GW of French grid connections — a power challenge the announcement does not yet solve.
articles.body_md:
**SoftBank Group**'s announcement at **Emmanuel Macron**'s "Choose France" summit on May 30, 2026, commits up to **€75B** to build and operate **5 GW** of AI data centre capacity in France — the largest announced foreign direct investment in French modern economic history and the biggest single AI infrastructure pledge in Europe.

## The Phase 1 Commitment

The confirmed capital is **€45B** for **3.1 GW** across three sites in Hauts-de-France: Dunkirk (Loon-Plage), Bosquel, and Bouchain, targeted ready-for-service by 2031. A Phase 2 extension of €30B is contingent on Phase 1 execution. At 5 GW total, the commitment represents more colocation-equivalent capacity than France, Germany, and the Netherlands currently operate in aggregate.

The Hauts-de-France geography is infrastructure-rational: North Sea cable landing proximity for hyperscaler traffic routing, industrial land cost advantages over the Paris metro, and cross-Channel interconnect access to the UK market. The industrial partnership is a strategic differentiator: **Schneider Electric** will co-locate manufacturing at Port of Dunkirk — SoftBank producing enclosures, Schneider assembling DC power modules — creating an in-country supply chain that addresses French digital sovereignty concerns and reduces lead-time exposure for subsequent phases.

## The Power Question the Announcement Does Not Answer

**5 GW at typical PUE requires approximately 5 TWh/year** — a power volume that exceeds the annual electricity consumption of several French departments. SoftBank has disclosed no PPA arrangements or grid connection strategy for the Hauts-de-France sites. The same energy economics that paused **Stargate UK** indefinitely (Edition 6 — industrial electricity at 24.67p/kWh, ~4x US rates) apply in northern France. French industrial electricity costs, while below UK levels, remain materially above Norwegian (~€0.03–0.04/kWh) and Swedish (~€0.05/kWh) baseload rates that have made the Nordics Europe's AI compute anchor.

The political framing — **Masayoshi Son** alongside Macron — signals a bilateral partnership. "Choose France" commitments historically deploy on 5–10-year timescales. The 3.1 GW Phase 1 requires French grid connection approvals governed by **EDF** and **RTE** capacity allocation, not bilateral diplomatic momentum.

Watch: French grid connection applications at three Hauts-de-France sites; EDF or Engie PPA negotiations for the initial 3.1 GW power requirement; and whether Phase 1 delivery is anchored to specific hyperscaler or AI operator offtake agreements, which would substantially de-risk the announced timeline.
articles.summary: SoftBank Group announced €75B in AI data centre investment in France at Macron's Choose France summit, with €45B confirmed for 3.1 GW across three Hauts-de-France sites by 2031. The 5 GW total requiring ~5 TWh/year has no disclosed PPA or grid connection strategy.

articles.title: EU AI Gigafactory Bidder Pool Collapses to ~10: Procurement Friction vs. Private Capital Speed
articles.subtitle: Schwarz Group is building 200+ MW in Berlin independently — without waiting for the EU subsidy process.
articles.body_md:
The EU's **€20B AI gigafactory initiative** — five sovereign AI data centres designed to reduce European dependence on US hyperscaler infrastructure — is experiencing a structural confidence failure. Initial expressions of interest numbered approximately **70**. Expected July 2026 submissions: approximately **10**. At least two remaining consortia are considering withdrawal if the programme is significantly downsized.

## The Financing Structure That Has Failed

The programme's design assumed a **4:1 leverage ratio**: €4.1B in confirmed EU subsidy would unlock €15.9B from host member states and private co-investors. That assumption has not held. Only **2 of the 5** planned centres can receive EU funding before the 2028 EU budget cycle. Member states with the deepest pockets — Germany and France — are deploying capital independently: **SoftBank**'s €75B France partnership (this edition), **Microsoft**'s and **Google**'s bilateral European data centre commitments all circumvent the EU-governed pooling structure.

The **European Commission** deferred the bidding round from May 2026 to July 2026 after repeatedly delaying the publication of selection criteria. Procurement friction is compounding the financing gap.

## Schwarz Group's Independent Decision Is the Benchmark

**Schwarz Group** — the Lidl/Kaufland parent and Europe's largest retailer by revenue — has cooled its gigafactory interest, citing the "complex and lengthy tender process." It is instead building a **200+ MW data centre south of Berlin** without waiting for EU subsidy. This is the archetype of the programme's structural problem: private capital and large operators can build AI data centres faster, cheaper, and with clearer commercial logic than EU procurement rules permit. The EU subsidy process adds 12–18 months of procurement friction for a co-investment return that no longer justifies the delay when bilateral and unilateral routes are available.

## Redistribution, Not Demand Loss

For infrastructure investors, the gigafactory programme's retreat does not reduce European AI data centre demand. It redistributes it toward bilateral investment structures — national summits, Microsoft/Google bilateral capex, SoftBank France — and away from EU-governed processes, accelerating a fragmentation of European AI infrastructure governance already visible in Italy's **TIM Sparkle** nationalisation (Edition 13) and Ireland's CRU generation obligation (Edition 10).

Watch: July 2026 deadline and confirmed submission count; whether the Commission downsizes to 3 centres to concentrate the €4.1B EU commitment; and **Schwarz Group**'s Berlin timeline as the private-sector benchmark against the subsidised programme.
articles.summary: The EU's €20B AI gigafactory initiative has seen its bidder pool collapse from ~70 expressions of interest to ~10 expected submissions, with the bidding round deferred to July 2026. Only €4.1B of the €20B programme has confirmed EU funding, and the €15.9B co-investment from member states has not materialised.

articles.title: 17 Nations Form GUIDE: The First Multilateral Framework for Subsea Cable Defence
articles.subtitle: UK armed forces tracked 3 Russian submarines surveying North Atlantic cable routes the same week GUIDE launched in Singapore.
articles.body_md:
Seventeen nations formally established that submarine cable security is a defence-coordination priority on May 30, 2026, launching **GUIDE** (Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defence Exchanges) at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore — the first cross-regional framework for undersea cable security.

## Founding Members and Geographic Scope

GUIDE's founding members include **7 EU member states** — Estonia, Finland, France, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Netherlands, and Sweden — plus the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia, Philippines, Qatar, and Thailand. The geographic coverage is deliberate: these 17 nations collectively oversee cable infrastructure at the Atlantic, Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific chokepoints facing active disruption — the same corridors tracked in this briefing since the **17-cable Red Sea disruption** (Edition 1), Iran's Hormuz cable mandate (Edition 12), and Baltic Sea surveillance activity.

GUIDE is voluntary and non-binding — no financial commitments, no enforcement mechanism. It operates as structured information-sharing for early warning of cable security incidents and standardised best-practice exchange.

## The Intelligence Context That Makes GUIDE Operational

GUIDE's significance is not its binding authority — it has none. It is the geopolitical scope combined with the concurrent intelligence disclosed. UK Defence Secretary confirmed that UK armed forces tracked **3 Russian submarines operating covertly in the North Atlantic specifically to survey subsea cable routes** in the same week GUIDE launched. Early warning of surveying activity is only actionable if there is a pre-agreed mechanism to share and respond — which is precisely what GUIDE provides.

GUIDE now operates in parallel with the **EU Cable Security Toolbox** and the **€347M CEF Digital cable security programme** (Edition 14), creating dual governance frameworks for the same physical infrastructure: military/intelligence coordination (GUIDE) and civilian/infrastructure investment (EU CEF). If 7 EU member states are sharing military surveillance of cable routes with Indo-Pacific partners, the case for the EU's **€180M backbone call** and **€20M Baltic Sea emergency repair** capacity is materially easier to justify to national finance ministries.

## Implications for Cable Operators and Investors

For cable operators and infrastructure investors, GUIDE creates two near-term practical implications: enhanced government-to-operator information flow on credible threats, and a more direct channel to host-government support for emergency repair coordination — a gap identified repeatedly through the Red Sea and Hormuz disruption episodes.

Watch: whether GUIDE expands to include the US, Japan, or South Korea (currently absent despite critical cable infrastructure holdings); whether voluntary principles evolve toward binding bilateral cable security agreements; and how GUIDE's early warning information interacts with commercial cable operator repair vessel deployment decisions.
articles.summary: Seventeen nations launched GUIDE at the Shangri-La Dialogue on May 30, establishing the first cross-regional information-sharing framework for undersea cable security, covering Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Indo-Pacific chokepoints. The UK simultaneously disclosed tracking 3 Russian submarines surveying North Atlantic cable routes.

articles.title: UK's 125 GW Grid Queue: 50 GW Tied to Data Centres, Ofgem Proposes Financial Gatekeeping
articles.subtitle: Ofgem proposes deposits, commitment fees, and FID evidence to clear 50 GW of speculative data centre queue entries.
articles.body_md:
The UK electricity demand connection queue tripled in seven months: **41 GW** in November 2024 to **125 GW** by June 2025, with approximately **50 GW** linked to data centre projects. **Ofgem**'s Phase 1 demand connection reform — with data centres as the explicit focus — proposes financial gatekeeping measures designed to clear speculative queue entries and accelerate connections for committed infrastructure projects.

## Why 125 GW Is a Dysfunction Signal, Not a Demand Signal

**NESO** analysis identifies approximately **140 data centres** in the connection queue, of which only 71 (~20 GW) have reached Final Investment Decision. The majority of queued data centre capacity is pre-FID or speculative — reserving grid headroom without deploying real load. A queue representing three times the UK's total installed generation capacity creates a negative externality for every genuine infrastructure project: congestion delays connection timelines for operators with committed capital and secured planning approval.

Ofgem's proposed Phase 1 measures include refundable deposits tied to delivery milestones, progressive commitment fees, evidence of secured financing, and outline planning permission as queue entry conditions. For data centre operators with genuine FIDs and secured financing, the reforms are net positive: speculative entries withdraw, genuine queue positions accelerate.

## The tCSNP2 Refresh Is the More Consequential Document

The **tCSNP2 refresh** — the UK transmission network investment plan — is due this month. It will establish which transmission corridors receive investment, on what timeline, and for what load volumes, directly determining where data centre development is grid-capable in 2028–2032. Ofgem's Phase 1 prioritisation signals will likely favour projects in government-designated AI Growth Zones and projects with **NSIP** planning approval (Edition 12), giving those developments a grid connection processing advantage.

Combined with the NSIP planning reform, **Ofcom**'s expanded cybersecurity oversight via the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, and Ofgem's Phase 1 reform, the UK's data centre regulatory architecture is converging toward greater structure in 2026. The structural constraint that none of these reforms address remains: industrial electricity at **24.67p/kWh** — approximately 5x Norway and 2x Sweden — which continues to direct greenfield AI infrastructure investment toward Nordic geographies.

Watch: Ofgem's formal Phase 1 decision publication; tCSNP2 refresh content and which transmission corridors are prioritised; whether any data centre developer challenges the financial gatekeeping requirements in judicial review, as Ireland's analogous CRU generation obligation is currently being challenged by environmental groups (Edition 14).
articles.summary: The UK electricity connection queue tripled to 125 GW in seven months, with ~50 GW linked to data centre projects — of which only 71 of ~140 queued DCs have reached Final Investment Decision. Ofgem's Phase 1 reform proposes financial gatekeeping to clear speculative entries, while the tCSNP2 transmission plan refresh due this month will set the grid-capable corridors for 2028–2032.
